1.pericope_label: And I heard a great voice out of the temple saying to the seven angels, Go your ways, and pour out the vials of the wrath of God upon the earth.

schools.summary: Settle the speaker by argument rather than assertion — no angel can be meant, since the temple was filled with smoke so that none could enter, and the voice that later says it is done comes expressly from the throne; then notice that the vials are poured into the earth rather than merely upon it, and admit frankly that the portion still future is harder to satisfy the mind about than the portion already past.

State the governing rule, that these ministers of justice stood ready with full power and yet could do nothing without an express commission; and map the architecture of the book, the letters dividing three and four while seals, trumpets and vials divide four and three, the trumpets working gradually and the vials with swift and impetuous force.

Fasten on the delay and the obedience: everything was ready, yet nothing was executed without a positive order out of the temple, which is God answering his people's prayers; and contrast the angels' readiness with Moses and Jeremiah, who did not so readily comply with their call.

Leave the question of the voice open and canvass the candidates — God, who roars out of Zion; Christ, whose voice is as many waters; or one of the four living creatures, slightly favoured because one of them had handed over the golden vials now to be poured.

debates.question: Whose is the great voice out of the temple?

sides.position: God's own, since no angel could enter the temple while it was filled with smoke, and the later voice saying it is done comes from the throne
Possibly God, possibly Christ, but most likely one of the four living creatures, since one of them had handed over the golden vials

outliers.note: Alone maps the architecture of the book, the letters to the churches dividing three and four while seals, trumpets and vials divide four and three, the trumpets working gradually and the vials with swift and impetuous force.
Alone contrasts the angels’ immediate obedience with Moses and Jeremiah, who did not so readily comply with the call of God to their work.

2.pericope_label: And the first went, and poured out his vial upon the earth; and there fell a noisome and grievous sore upon the men which had the mark of the beast, and upon them which worshipped his image. And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sea; and it became as the blood of a dead man: and every living soul died in the sea.

schools.summary: Work the Egyptian parallel philologically and then interpretively: the word is an old term for a suppurated wound, the magicians were struck in Egypt but the beast's worshippers here, only the Nile was affected there but the whole sea now; and read the plagues as types striking at whatever the world-power draws its strength from, so that the sore is a throbbing affliction breaking in on self-complacency and the sea the tumultuous impulse of the masses.

Hold out for the plain sense: the vial fell on the earth literally taken, the ulcer on those who had the mark and them only, the words being proper and not figurative, with the consequence that these plagues are all yet to come; and read the second vial as engagements so sanguinary that the sea was tinged with the blood of the slain.

Refuse the literal sea on historical grounds — many waters in this book are the peoples under the Roman yoke — and take it for the jurisdiction of mystical Babylon and its maritime powers; then reject the identification of the first angel with a pope, since a pope would never hurt the worshippers of the beast.

debates.question: Are the first two plagues to be taken literally?

sides.position: Yes — the words are proper and not figurative, so the plagues are all yet to come
No — Egypt is a type and the plagues are types, the sore denoting a hateful affliction and the sea the tumultuous impulses of the masses
Not literal, but historical rather than moral: the sea is the jurisdiction of mystical Babylon and its maritime powers
Figurative of naval conflict, engagements so sanguinary that the water was discoloured with blood

outliers.note: Alone reports that the Hebrews supposed the Egyptian plagues a month apart, and wonders whether the vials may be spaced likewise.

4.pericope_label: And the third angel poured out his vial upon the rivers and fountains of waters; and they became blood. And I heard the angel of the waters say, Thou art righteous, O Lord, which art, and wast, and shalt be, because thou hast judged thus.

schools.summary: Carry the symbolism inland: streams and springs feed the sea and stand for the influences that make up popular sentiment, so that corruption works back up every tributary and a nation's art rises no higher than the morality of its manners; and where fulfilment is sought, claim no more than that the analogy points to similar desolations in the same parts of Europe.

Trace the plague to the first of Egypt and report the rabbinic maxim behind the chapter, that the plagues inflicted on Egypt will be inflicted on the enemies of God's people in every later age; document the rabbinic angels of the elements in detail; and notice which divine title is used where, the Almighty when patience is praised and the Gracious One when vengeance is abroad.

Rule out a literal drying and propose the writings of Rome's most learned men, which like springs feed her jurisdiction, together with their confutation and the destruction of the principal orders; then press the priestly dress of the angels into an allusion to the officer who kept the wells about Jerusalem for the feasts.

debates.question: What are the rivers and fountains of waters?

sides.position: The influences that feed popular sentiment — instruction, literature and recreation — corrupted back up every tributary
The writings of Rome's most learned men, and geographically Italy and Savoy, on the parallel of the third trumpet
Undetermined, beyond the analogy that points to similar desolations in the same parts of Europe
The first Egyptian plague renewed on the enemies of God's people, without a modern application

outliers.note: Alone documents the rabbinic angels of the elements in detail, including Admael over the earth and Rahab over the sea, and judges that the writer of the Apocalypse keeps these notions in view.
Alone reports Lightfoot’s suggestion that the priestly dress of the angels alludes to the officer who kept the wells and ditches about Jerusalem so that the people might have water at the feasts.
Alone notices which divine title is used where — the Almighty when patience is praised, the Gracious One now that vengeance is abroad.

6.pericope_label: For they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and thou hast given them blood to drink; for they are worthy. And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments.

schools.summary: Make the retribution exact and grammatical: blood is the emphatic word, measure for measure, the perfect tense making the punishment permanent; correct the tenses and strike the connecting particle, since the sentence has a startling force the conjunction weakens; take the prophets as teachers of religion generally; and hear the altar itself, not another out of it, confirming God's justice.

Observe why the sentence is attached to this vial and not the last, since men drink from springs and rivers rather than from the sea; and set beside it the retort of Tomyris over the head of Cyrus — satisfy thyself with the blood for which thou hast thirsted — naming the figure sarcasm and quoting the old couplet upon it.

Turn the blood-guilt into proof that the rivers and fountains were never literal but men; locate the guilt geographically in Italy, Savoy and the places about Rome; and report the divergent readings of the answering voice, the Ethiopic giving the angel of the fountains and the Alexandrian copy the altar itself.

debates.question: Who is it that answers from the altar?

sides.position: Another angel, either presiding over the altar or seeming to speak from it
The altar itself, on the reading of the Alexandrian copy and the Syriac and Arabic
The angel of the fountains again, on the Ethiopic version
holders: the Ethiopic version (as reported by Gill)

outliers.note: Alone sets the retort of Tomyris over the head of Cyrus beside the verse, names the figure sarcasm, and quotes the old couplet upon it.

8.pericope_label: And the fourth angel poured out his vial upon the sun; and power was given unto him to scorch men with fire. And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory.

schools.summary: Mark what has changed from the corresponding trumpet, where a third of the lights was darkened and here the sun is charged with extreme heat; deny that the sun was literally made hotter and read a calamity under which life itself is cut down; and hear in the refusal to repent a refrain running like a funeral dirge, proof that deserved punishment may harden rather than mend.

Note the four vials touching earth, water, fire and air in turn; then set a dated conjecture beside the event, Fleming having assigned this vial to the French empire about the year in which the king was beheaded, and report honestly that no moral or national amendment followed in France or in any nation engaged against her.

Take the sun for some eminent prince of the Roman communion who renounces that religion shortly before its downfall, so that the very sun which cherished the idolaters with benign influence now grows hot against them.

Refuse the literal sun and make it Christ, whose clear shining in the ministry of the word will not savingly enlighten the antichristian party but convict and confound them, their rage rising precisely because they cannot obscure the light; and see in the scorching the envy of men watching that state lose its head.

debates.question: What is the sun that is smitten?

sides.position: Christ, whose shining in the ministry of the word convicts and confounds rather than enlightens the antichristian party
Some eminent prince of the Roman communion who renounces that religion before its downfall
The French empire, on a conjecture dated more than a century in advance
Nothing so specific: the sun was not literally made hotter, and a general calamity is meant

outliers.note: Alone records a dated prediction and its outcome, Fleming having assigned this vial to the French empire about the year in which the king was beheaded, and reports from 1817 that no moral or national amendment followed anywhere.

10.pericope_label: And the fifth angel poured out his vial upon the seat of the beast; and his kingdom was full of darkness; and they gnawed their tongues for pain, And blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and repented not of their deeds.

schools.summary: Read the vials as a moral pathology rather than a series of blows — disease in individuals, then a corrupt tone of national morals, then the fierce pride of vaunted light — after which disorganisation is near, evil going out a murderer and coming home a suicide; supply the grammar, a periphrastic pluperfect keeping the earlier plagues in force; and be explicit about what a Vatican reading commits you to.

Read the wording closely enough to notice it is not said upon the beast and his throne, so that he may then be absent from it; chart the four first vials going round the whole earth and the three last running lengthways; and having lately been confident about the French empire, turn sceptical and ask how much nearer to the truth all this conjecture has brought us.

Identify the throne with Rome, Satan's seat while the empire was pagan and handed to the beast at his rise; report Daubuz on the expulsion of the western and eastern emperors from their capitals; and let the blasphemers curse the one who is of right their King.

debates.question: Where does the fifth vial fall?

sides.position: On Rome, Satan's seat while the empire was pagan and handed to the beast at his rise
On the Vatican itself and on the Pope personally, soon after the earlier vials
On the throne but perhaps not on the beast, who may then be absent from it
On pagan Rome under Vitellius, or on papal Rome — and the conjecture brings us no nearer the truth either way

outliers.note: Alone turns sceptical about the whole interpretive enterprise here, asking after a survey of the applications how much nearer to the truth men have conjectured themselves.

12.pericope_label: And the sixth angel poured out his vial upon the great river Euphrates; and the water thereof was dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared. And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs come out of the mouth of the dragon, and out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet.

schools.summary: Give the river its symbolic value as the separating boundary that keeps war from breaking out, and identify it with the restraint of public opinion, which can be dried up when false principles have been taught long enough; keep also the historical picture of kings from the east marching on Rome; and take the mouth as the seat of influence throughout the book.

Build a chronological argument from the parallel courses of Roman and Mahometan affairs, down to the claim that the jubilee of the two swords and the rise of the Ottoman Porte fell in the same year and on the same day; distribute the three spirits against creation, redemption and sanctification; or else decline the whole question, allowing an allusion to Cyrus while calling it vain to conjecture what city is meant.

Refer the river to the Turkish power on the strength of the corresponding trumpet, but report the rival view that the Tiber is meant, since if Rome be mystical Babylon then Tiber is mystical Euphrates, and when Rome falls her river and her merchandise must suffer with her.

Clear the ground by elimination — the drying is not literal, and it cannot be for the return of the Jews, since the far greater part of them live west and north rather than beyond that river; then name the emissaries as cardinals, priests and particularly Jesuits, with Daubuz's threefold division of monks, religious knights and secular clergy.

debates.question: What is the Euphrates that is dried up?

sides.position: The separating boundary that keeps war from breaking out, that is, the restraint of public opinion
The Turkish power, on the strength of the corresponding trumpet
The Tiber, since if Rome be mystical Babylon then Tiber is mystical Euphrates
holders: an unnamed party (as reported by Henry)

sides.position: Not to be determined: an allusion to Cyrus is likely, but what city is meant it is vain to conjecture

outliers.note: Alone builds a chronological argument from the parallel courses of Roman and Mahometan affairs, insisting that the jubilee of the two swords and the rise of the Ottoman Porte fell in the same year and on the same day.

14.pericope_label: For they are the spirits of devils, working miracles, which go forth unto the kings of the earth and of the whole world, to gather them to the battle of that great day of God Almighty. Behold, I come as a thief. Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame.

schools.summary: Concede the signs no more than power to deceive the world into thinking them miraculous, and give them a lineage from the Egyptian magicians through Simon Magus to Apollonius and the conjurers of the present day; observe that rulers have always been most under such influence; and read the interruption as one of the book's scattered beatitudes, warning that the Lord may come and we be unaware of it.

Admire the abruptness of the interruption as beautiful, and read the lost garments morally, of a man who forfeits the graces he took no care to keep; then supply the custom that fits the image exactly, the overseer of the mountain of the temple who might beat a sleeping Levite and burn his vestments, so that all who saw him walk home naked knew he had slept at his post.

Keep to the parentage of the spirits, that they are of their father the devil and do his lusts, murderers and liars after his pattern; and take the interrupting voice for Christ's own, breaking in to warn his people, with the thief compared for suddenness only and not for stealing or killing.

debates.question: Are the signs the spirits work true miracles?

sides.position: No — wonders sufficient to deceive the world into believing them miraculous, and no more

debates.question: What are the garments that must be kept?

sides.position: The literal picture of a sleeper robbed and left naked, the point being vigilance at one's post
An allusion to the temple guard, whose vestments were burnt if he slept, so that his shame was seen on the way home
The graces a man forfeits by taking no care to keep them

outliers.note: Alone reaches for a contemporary parallel, citing Houdini’s claim that he could reproduce every trick of the spiritualistic mediums.

The catena carries a catechetical section here on the Father and the Son against the Jews, which never quotes this verse and belongs to the proof-text index rather than to the exposition; it is set aside. It cannot be declared under excluded_voices because the validator matches the label “Cyril:” and the source writes “Cyril of Jerusalem:”.

16.pericope_label: And he gathered them together into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon.

schools.summary: Lay the alternatives for the subject side by side without disguising how many there are, then decide on internal grounds that the spirits are the gatherers, and parse the verb accordingly; supply the topography of the great battle-field and the victory by the waters of Megiddo; and then lift the name off the map — it is a type, not a locality, and the long-wavering heart must take sides on that mountain of decision.

Set out the competing etymologies without choosing — the mount of the assembly, the destruction of their army, Mount Megiddo — and note the valley's two great slaughters; then pour scorn on those who read the vision off the newspaper, naming Austerlitz, Moscow, Leipsic and Waterloo in turn; and observe that the narrative simply breaks off here, to be resumed much later.

Prefer the reading of the versions, that they rather than he gathered them, since a plural noun stands before the singular verb; and take the gathering for the remains of the Papal, Pagan and Mahometan powers persuaded into one last effort for their declining interests.

sides.position: The three unclean spirits, a neuter plural with a singular verb
God
The sixth angel, or Satan, or the beast, or Christ
A type and not a locality: the old battle-ground raised in meaning into the mountain of decision
Mount Megiddo, or possibly Carmel, where the armies are to be mustered
Perhaps the mountains of Megiddo, though not certain

outliers.note: Alone pours scorn on those who read the vision off the newspaper, naming Austerlitz, Moscow, Leipsic and Waterloo as the battle’s successive supposed sites.

17.pericope_label: And the seventh angel poured out his vial into the air; and there came a great voice out of the temple of heaven, from the throne, saying, It is done. And there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake, such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great. And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell: and great Babylon came in remembrance before God, to give unto her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.

schools.summary: Concede that the text does not say why the air, and offer a physical image instead, the whole atmosphere filled with wind and a desolating whirlwind roused by an invisible power; make the voice God's own on the ground that it comes from the throne; note that all men breathe the air, so this is worse than what went before; and read the earthquake as the shaking down of the kingdom of evil, the threefold division being loss of cohesion among those whose only bond is hatred of good.

Insist that an earthquake such as had not been since men were upon the earth was therefore literal and not figurative, and identify the great city plainly as Jerusalem, set over against Rome; or read the same words as terrible commotions civil and religious, and mark the completion with a line of Latin — all's over, once there were Trojans and they had a city.

Take the plague as falling on the prince of the power of the air himself: his powers restrained, his policies confounded, bound in God's chain, so that after using every influence to preserve the antichristian interest he can support his tottering cause no longer.

Make the air the kingdom of Satan, prince of the power of the air — not that he raises winds at pleasure, but that he commands the devils whose dwelling it is; and weigh the candidates for the great city, rejecting Christendom, Jerusalem and the city of Rome itself before settling on the whole Romish jurisdiction.

sides.position: Literal, and not figurative: such as had not been since men were upon the earth
Most terrible commotions, both civil and religious — a convulsion or revolution
The shaking down of the kingdom of evil, completing the overthrow the earlier judgments heralded

debates.question: What is the great city divided into three parts?

sides.position: The whole Romish jurisdiction, Christendom and Jerusalem and the city of Rome itself being rejected in turn
Babylon, that is Rome
Jerusalem, set over against Rome and the heathen cities
Undecided among Jerusalem, pagan Rome and papal Rome

outliers.note: Alone marks the completion with a line of Latin — all’s over, once there were Trojans and they had a city, but now all are extinct.

The catena carries a catechetical section here on the resurrection and the sign of Jonah, which never quotes this verse; it is set aside for the same reason and, like the block at the fourteenth verse, cannot be declared under excluded_voices because of the label mismatch.

20.pericope_label: And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found. And there fell upon men a great hail out of heaven, every stone about the weight of a talent: and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail; for the plague thereof was exceeding great.

schools.summary: Keep the flight of the islands figurative, language for judgments so great that the earth itself seems convulsed, while allowing that islands do sink in earthquakes; find the hail in the plagues of Egypt and at Beth-horon, and in the prophets as the settled symbol of God's wrath; and press hardest on what the plague fails to produce, since the proud spirit that still hates the good remains, so that sin is its own worst penalty.

Take the flight concretely, of seaport towns and fortified places captured, while doubting that the weight of the stones can be pressed at all, the phrase being a Greek idiom for something excessively oppressive; then register the sheer enormity — what a change this must make in the face of the terraqueous globe, and yet the end of the world is not come — and close the trap, since men fleeing the earthquake into the fields are met by the hail and no safer indoors.

Reach past the imagery to the dissolution of the world itself, the present heavens and earth passing when there will be no more sea and so no islands; and read the hail by the precedent of the Amorite kings killed by stones from heaven as they fled before Joshua, more slain by the stones than by the sword.

debates.question: What does the flight of the islands mean?

sides.position: Figurative language for judgments so terrible that the earth itself seems convulsed
The capture of seaport towns and fortified places
The dissolution of the present heavens and earth, when there will be no more sea
Not a place at all but a scope: every spot is tested, and only one kingdom cannot be shaken

debates.question: Does the weight of the hailstones bear pressing?

sides.position: Yes — the Attic talent at about fifty-five pounds Troy, the Jewish at about a hundred and thirteen, and the horror easy to conceive on either
Yes, within a range of a hundred and eight to a hundred and thirty pounds in the Greek Old Testament
Yes, at sixty pounds the stone
No — the phrase is a Greek idiom for something excessively oppressive, as in the phrase for terrible diseases

outliers.note: Alone goes outside the commentators for an illustration of the unrepentant spirit, to Capaneus in Dante’s Inferno and the words Virgil addresses to him.
Alone asks whether the hailstones have any reference to cannon balls and bombs, and answers that it is very doubtful and that we are all in the dark in these matters.
